Hi Priya / Amit —

Thanks again for the call today. Quick recap + proposed next steps so we can keep momentum: 

Recap:
- Primary use case: real-time clinical documentation assistant integrated into their provider app; patients & clinicians need token-level streaming for near-instant UI updates.
- Key quality concerns: partial output coherence when responses are interrupted, respect for stop sequences (safety/formatting), and overall end-to-end latency targets (~<200ms per token from our runtime).
- Data: they will share a 3k sample of anonymized prompts and a few typical stop sequences (e.g., "

END NOTE", JSON-close tokens).

Redwood ask / next steps:
1) We’ll propose 1-2 recommended model variants (tradeoff table: latency vs. instruction-following quality).
2) Send over a prompt set + recommended stop-sequence handling and a link to our evaluation bench so they can review. (Attachment: acme_prompt_set_v2.json)
3) Quick follow-up call with engineering to validate streaming behavior and latency expectations — propose Wed or Thu next week.

Attached: acme_prompt_set_v2.json (sample prompts + stop sequences). I’m also attaching our initial benchmark notes (summary) in the next email.

Thanks Marissa — super helpful summary. A couple clarifications from our product team: 

- Latency target: ideally end-to-end UI token arrival < 200ms for the first visible tokens; we can tolerate slightly higher for subsequent tokens but want a responsive feel.
- Stop sequences: we have explicit markers we use in the UI (e.g., "END NOTE" and JSON delimiters). We need to be confident that partial streaming won’t produce invalid JSON fragments that confuse our parser.
- Regression concern: we had a previous vendor where a model update caused increased hallucination on truncated outputs; want to avoid the same.

Yes to a technical follow-up — Thu 07/02 in the morning Pacific works for us. Could you include some high-level recommended models and any benchmarks you have for streaming behavior ahead of that call?

—Amit

Marissa — thanks for looping us in. Quick engineering read + recommended next steps below.

Summary of recommended models (tradeoffs):
- redwood-rlhf-1.5b-v2-quant (recommended starter): very fast on our Dedicate/Hosted runtime with 8-bit quantized kernels; strong instruction-following and lower token-latency. Expected median first-token latency ~120-180ms in our region under typical load.
- open-llama-13b-q4f (higher quality fallback): better long-form coherence but ~2-3x token-latency; useful if Acme prioritizes fewer hallucinations over strict per-token latency.

Streaming / partial-output guidance:
- Stop-sequence enforcement: enable strict stop-sequence scanning on both the model output and streaming buffer. We recommend configuring an output-terminator buffer that buffers up to N=4 tokens before emitting if a stop-prefix is detected to avoid emitting incomplete stop sequences. This reduces risk of invalid JSON fragments.
- Stream checkpoints: enable our 'stream_checkpoint' option (we’ll demo). This emits an explicit end-of-sentence checkpoint token which the client can treat as a safe boundary for parsing.
- Partial-disable threshold: for JSON-heavy outputs, set partial_disable_threshold=0.25 so streaming degrades to chunked full-sentence emissions for the last 25% of expected tokens (helps prevent truncated JSON). We can tune this during the 50-prompt run.
- KV cache priming: prime with their typical few-shot examples to reduce divergences on short prompts. We’ll run through a subset of their sample prompts to confirm cache behavior.

Plan / ETA:
- I’ll run the 50-prompt streaming validation today and upload results to: https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/folders/streaming-evals-ACME-2026 (expect a short CSV + per-prompt recordings).
- Rishi will spin up the two candidate model variants on a small test harness; we should have initial numbers in ~6-8 hours.
- Recommend we keep the Thu morning slot for a joint demo; Marissa — can you confirm time with the customer?

Deliverables we’ll share before the demo:
1) Per-model latency and stop-sequence failure rate (CSV).
2) Example transcripts showing problematic partial outputs and the tuned config that resolved them.
3) A short checklist for the customer’s client-side parser to safely consume streaming output (we’ll draft).

If any of this changes the ask let me know — otherwise I’ll post the validation results to the linked Drive later today.

—Jordan
